entries.3af383e56d090e0afd8d9f4a00bbc75ab57323d2: <div sID="gen12566" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="115" osisID="Ps.115" sID="Ps.115"/> <div eID="gen12566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12567" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12568" type="x-p"/> Many ancient translations join this psalm to that which goes next before it, the Septuagint particularly, and the vulgar Latin; but it is, in the Hebrew, a distinct psalm. In it we are taught to give glory, I. To God, and not to ourselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. To God, and not to idols, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2-Ps.115.8">ver. 2-8</reference>. We must give glory to God, 1. By trusting in him, and in his promise and blessing, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.15">ver. 9-15</reference>. 2. By blessing him, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.16-Ps.115.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. Some think this psalm was penned upon occasion of some great distress and trouble that the church of God was in, when the enemies were in insolent and threatening, in which case the church does not so much pour out her complaint to God as place her confidence in God, and triumph in doing so; and with such a holy triumph we ought to sing this psalm.
entries.c5759907fdc78d136f3c92ee380becec2e94cd39: <div eID="gen12568" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12567" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Absurdity of Idolatry.</title> <div sID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Not unto us, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, <hi type="italic">and</hi> for thy truth's sake. <hi type="super">2</hi> Wherefore should the heathen say, Where <hi type="italic">is</hi> now their God? <hi type="super">3</hi> But our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased. <hi type="super">4</hi> Their idols <hi type="italic">are</hi> silver and gold, the work of men's hands. <hi type="super">5</hi> They have mouths, but they speak not: eyes have they, but they see not: <hi type="super">6</hi> They have ears, but they hear not: noses have they, but they smell not: <hi type="super">7</hi> They have hands, but they handle not: feet have they, but they walk not: neither speak they through their throat. <hi type="super">8</hi> They that make them are like unto them; <hi type="italic">so is</hi> every one that trusteth in them. <div eID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> Sufficient care is here taken to answer both the pretensions of self and the reproaches of idolaters. <div eID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> I. Boasting is here for ever excluded, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1">v. 1</reference>. Let no opinion of our own merits have any room either in our prayers or in our praises, but let both centre in God's glory. 1. Have we received any mercy, gone through any service, or gained any success? We must not assume the glory of it to ourselves, but ascribe it wholly to God. We must not imagine that we do any thing for God by our own strength, or deserve any thing from God by our own righteousness; but all the good we do is done by the power of his grace, and all the good we have is the gift of his mere mercy, and therefore he must have all the praise. Say not, <hi type="italic">The power of my hand has gotten me this wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 17</reference>. Say not, <hi type="italic">For my righteousness the Lord has</hi> done these great and kind things for me, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4">Deut. ix. 4</reference>. No; all our songs must be sung to this humble tune, <hi type="italic">Not unto us, O Lord!</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Not unto us, but to thy name,</hi> let all the glory be given; for whatever good is wrought in us, or wrought for us, it is for his mercy and his truth's sake, because he will glorify his mercy and fulfil his promise. All our crowns must be cast at the feet of <hi type="italic">him that sits upon the throne,</hi> for that is the proper place for them. 2. Are we in pursuit of any mercy and wrestling with God for it? We must take our encouragement, in prayer, from God only, and have an eye to his glory more than to our own benefit in it. "Lord, do so and so for us, not that we may have the credit and comfort of it, but that thy mercy and truth may have the glory of it." This must be our highest and ultimate end in our prayers, and therefore it is made the first petition in the Lord's prayer, as that which guides all the rest, <hi type="italic">Hallowed be thy name;</hi> and, in order to that, <hi type="italic">Give us our daily bread,</hi> &c. This also must satisfy us, if our prayers be not answered in the letter of them. Whatever becomes of us, <hi type="italic">unto thy name give glory.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.12.27-John.12.28">John xii. 27, 28</reference>. <div eID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12572" type="x-p"/> II. The reproach of the heathen is here for ever silenced and justly retorted. <div eID="gen12572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12573" type="x-p"/> 1. The psalmist complains of the reproach of the heathen (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore should they say, Where is now their God?</hi> (1.) "Why do they say so? Do they not know that our God is every where by his providence, and always nigh to us by his promise and grace?" (2.) "Why does God permit them to say so? Nay, why is Israel brought so low that they have some colour for saying so? Lord, appear for our relief, that thou mayest vindicate thyself, and glorify thy own name." <div eID="gen12573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12574" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives a direct answer to their question, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">v. 3</reference>. "Do they ask where is our God? We can tell where he is." (1.) "In the upper world is the presence of his glory: <hi type="italic">Our God is in the heavens,</hi> where the gods of the heathen never were, <hi type="italic">in the heavens,</hi> and therefore out of sight; but, though his majesty be unapproachable, it does not therefore follow that his being is questionable." (2.) "In the lower world are the products of his power: <hi type="italic">He has done whatsoever he pleased,</hi> according to the counsel of his will; he has a sovereign dominion and a universal uncontrollable influence. Do you ask where he is? He is at the beginning and end of every thing, <hi type="italic">and not far from any of us.</hi>" <div eID="gen12574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12575" type="x-p"/> 3. He returns their question upon themselves. They asked, Where is the God of Israel? because he is not seen. He does in effect ask, What are the gods of the heathen? because they are seen. (1.) He shows that their gods, though they are not shapeless things, are senseless things. Idolaters, at first, worshipped the sun and moon (<reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job xxxi. 26</reference>), which was bad enough, but not so bad as that which they were now come to (for evil men grow worse and worse), which was the worshipping of images, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.4">v. 4</reference>. The matter of them was <hi type="italic">silver and gold,</hi> dug out of the earth (<hi type="italic">man found them poor and dirty in a mine,</hi> Herbert), proper things to make money of, but not to make gods of. The make of them was from the artificer; they are creatures of men's vain imaginations and <hi type="italic">the works of men's hands,</hi> and therefore can have no divinity in them. If man is the work of God's hands (as certainly he is, and it was his honour that he was made <hi type="italic">in the image of God</hi>) it is absurd to think that that can be God which is the work of men's hands, or that it can be any other than a dishonour to God to make him in the image of man. The argument is irrefragable: <hi type="italic">The workmen made it, therefore it is not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">Hos. viii. 6</reference>. These idols are represented here as the most ridiculous things, a mere jest, that would seem to be something, but were really nothing, fitter for a toy shop than a temple, for children to play with than for men to pray to. The painter, the carver, the statuary, did their part well enough; they made them with <hi type="italic">mouths</hi> and <hi type="italic">eyes, ears</hi> and <hi type="italic">noses, hands</hi> and <hi type="italic">feet,</hi> but they could put no life into them and therefore no sense. They had better have worshipped a dead carcase (for that had life in it once) than a dead image, which neither has life nor can have. <hi type="italic">They speak not,</hi> in answer to those that consult them; the crafty priest must speak for them. In Baal's image there was <hi type="italic">no voice, neither any that answered. They see not</hi> the prostrations of their worshippers before them, much less their burdens and wants. <hi type="italic">They hear not</hi> their prayers, though ever so loud; <hi type="italic">they smell not</hi> their incense, though ever so strong, ever so sweet; <hi type="italic">they handle not</hi> the gifts presented to them, much less have they any gifts to bestow on their worshippers; they cannot <hi type="italic">stretch forth their hands to the needy. They walk not,</hi> they cannot stir a step for the relief of those that apply to them. Nay, they do not so much as <hi type="italic">breathe through their throat;</hi> they have not the least sign of symptom of life, but are as dead, after the priest has pretended to consecrate them and call a deity into them, as they were before. (2.) He thence infers the sottishness of their worshippers (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that make them</hi> images show their ingenuity, and doubtless are sensible men; but <hi type="italic">those that make them</hi> gods show their stupidity and folly, and <hi type="italic">are like unto them,</hi> as senseless blockish things; <hi type="italic">they see not</hi> the invisible things of the true and living God in the works of creation; <hi type="italic">they hear not</hi> the voice of the day and the night, which in every speech and language declare his glory, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.2-Ps.19.3">Ps. xix. 2, 3</reference>. By worshipping these foolish puppets, they make themselves more and more foolish like them, and set themselves at a greater distance from every thing that is spiritual, sinking themselves deeper into the mire of sense; and withal they provoke God to <hi type="italic">give them up to a reprobate mind, a mind void of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom. i. 28</reference>. Those <hi type="italic">that trust in them</hi> act very absurdly and very unreasonably, are senseless, helpless, useless, like them; and they will find it so themselves, to their own confusion. We shall know where our God is, and so shall they, to their cost, when their gods are gone, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.3-Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 3-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa. xliv. 9</reference>, &c.
entries.d5f41c9248fac66a841decf3021962f616516beb: <div eID="gen12575" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen12576" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> O Israel, trust thou in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he <hi type="italic">is</hi> their help and their shield. 10 O house of Aaron, trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he <hi type="italic">is</hi> their help and their shield. 11 Ye that fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he <hi type="italic">is</hi> their help and their shield. <hi type="super">12</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath been mindful of us: he will bless <hi type="italic">us;</hi> he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron. <hi type="super">13</hi> He will bless them that fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">both</hi> small and great. <hi type="super">14</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall increase you more and more, you and your children. <hi type="super">15</hi> Ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> blessed of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which made heaven and earth. <hi type="super">16</hi> The heaven, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the heavens, <hi type="italic">are</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men. <hi type="super">17</hi> The dead praise not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , neither any that go down into silence. <hi type="super">18</hi> But we will bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from this time forth and for evermore. Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12577" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen12577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12578" type="x-p"/> I. We are earnestly exhorted, all of us, to repose our confidence in God, and not suffer our confidence in him to be shaken by the heathens' insulting over us upon the account of our present distresses. It is folly to trust in dead images, but it is wisdom to trust in the living God, for he is a <hi type="italic">help and a shield</hi> to those that do <hi type="italic">trust in them,</hi> a help to furnish them with and forward them in that which is good, and a shield to fortify them against and protect them from every thing that is evil. Therefore, 1. Let Israel trust in the Lord; the body of the people, as to their public interests, and every particular Israelite, as to his own private concerns, let them leave it to God to dispose of all for them, and believe it will dispose of all for the best and will be <hi type="italic">their help and shield.</hi> 2. Let the priests, the Lord's ministers, and all the families of the <hi type="italic">house of Aaron, trust in the Lord,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.10">v. 10</reference>); they are most maligned and struck at by the enemies and therefore of them God takes particular care. They ought to be examples to others of a cheerful confidence in God, and a faithful adherence to him in the worst of times. 3. Let the proselytes, who are not of the seed of Israel, but <hi type="italic">fear the Lord,</hi> who worship him and make conscience of their duty to him, let them <hi type="italic">trust in him,</hi> for he will not fail nor forsake them, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.11">v. 11</reference>. Note, Wherever there is an awful fear of God, there may be a cheerful faith in him: those that reverence his word may rely upon it. <div eID="gen12578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12579" type="x-p"/> II. We are greatly encouraged to trust in God, and good reason is given us why we should stay ourselves upon him with an entire satisfaction. Consider, 1. What we have experienced (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has been mindful of us,</hi> and never unmindful, has been so constantly, has been so remarkably upon special occasions. He has been mindful of our case, our wants and burdens, mindful of our prayers to him, his promises to us, and the covenant-relation between him and us. All our comforts are derived from God's <hi type="italic">thoughts to us-ward;</hi> he <hi type="italic">has been mindful of us,</hi> though we have forgotten him. Let <hi type="italic">this</hi> engage us to trust in him, that we have found him faithful. 2. What we may expect. From what he has done for us we may infer, <hi type="italic">He will bless us;</hi> he that has been our <hi type="italic">help and our shield</hi> will be so; he that has <hi type="italic">remembered us in our low estate</hi> will not forget us; for he is still the same, his power and goodness the same, and his promise inviolable; so that we have reason to hope that he who has delivered, and does, will yet deliver. Yet this is not all: <hi type="italic">He will bless us;</hi> he has promised that he will; he has pronounced a blessing upon all his people. God's blessing us is not only speaking good to us, but doing well for us; those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. It is particularly promised that <hi type="italic">he will bless the house of Israel,</hi> that is, he will bless the commonwealth, will bless his people in their civil interests. <hi type="italic">He will bless the house of Aaron,</hi> that is, the church, the ministry, will bless his people in their religious concerns. The priests were to bless the people; it was their office (<reference osisRef="Num.6.23">Num. vi. 23</reference>); but God blessed them, and so blessed their blessings. Nay (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">he will bless those that fear the Lord,</hi> though they be not of the house of Israel or the house of Aaron; for it was a truth, before Peter perceived it, <hi type="italic">That in every nation he that fears God is accepted or him,</hi> and blessed, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.34-Acts.10.35">Acts x. 34, 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">He will bless them both small and great,</hi> both young and old. God has blessings in store for those that are good betimes and for those that are old disciples, both those that are poor in the world and those that make a figure. The greatest need his blessing, and it shall not be denied to the meanest that fear him. Both the weak in grace and the strong shall be blessed of God, the lambs and the sheep of his flock. It is promised (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord shall increase you.</hi> Whom God blesses he increases; that was one of the earliest and most ancient blessings, <hi type="italic">Be fruitful and multiply.</hi> God's blessing gives an increase—increase in number, building up the family—increase in wealth, adding to the estate and honour—especially an increase in spiritual blessings, with the increasings of God. He will bless you with the increase of knowledge and wisdom, of grace, holiness, and joy; those are blessed indeed whom God thus increases, who are made wiser and better, and fitter for God and heaven. It is promised that this shall be, (1.) A constant continual increase: "<hi type="italic">He shall increase you more and more;</hi> so that, as long as you live, you shall be still increasing, till you come to perfection, as the shining light," <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Prov. iv. 18</reference>. (2.) An hereditary increase: "<hi type="italic">You and your children;</hi> you in your children." It is a comfort to parents to see their children increasing in wisdom and strength. There is a blessing entailed upon the seed of those that fear God even in their infancy. For (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.15">v. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">You are blessed of the Lord,</hi> you and your children are so; <hi type="italic">all that see them shall acknowledge them, that they are the seed which the Lord has blessed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.9">Isa. lix. 9</reference>. Those that are the blessed of the Lord have encouragement enough to <hi type="italic">trust in the Lord,</hi> as <hi type="italic">their help and shield,</hi> for it is he that <hi type="italic">made heaven and earth;</hi> therefore his blessings are free, for he needs not any thing himself; and therefore they are rich, for he has all things at command for us if we fear him and trust in him. He that <hi type="italic">made heaven and earth</hi> can doubtless make those happy that trust in him, and will do it. <div eID="gen12579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12580" type="x-p"/> III. We are stirred up to praise God by the psalmist's example, who concludes the psalm with a resolution to persevere in his praises. 1. God is to be praised, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.16">v. 16</reference>. He is greatly to be praised; for, (1.) His glory is high. See how stately his palace is, and the throne he has prepared in the heavens: <hi type="italic">The heaven, even the heavens are the Lord's;</hi> he is the rightful owner of all the treasures of light and bliss in the upper and better world, and is in the full possession of them, for he is himself infinitely bright and happy. (2.) His goodness is large, for <hi type="italic">the earth he has given to the children of men,</hi> having designed it, when he made it, for their use, to find them with meat, drink, and lodging. Not but that still he is proprietor in chief; <hi type="italic">the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof;</hi> but he has let out that vineyard to these unthankful husbandmen, and from them he expects the rents and services; for, though he has given them the earth, his eye is upon them, and he will call them to render an account how they use it. Calvin complains that profane wicked people, in his days, perverted this scripture, and made a jest of it, which some in our days do, arguing, in banter, that God, having given the earth to the children of men, will no more look after it, nor after them upon it, but they may do what they will with it, and make the best of it as their portion; it is as it were thrown like a prey among them, Let him seize it that can. It is a pity that such an instance as this gives of God's bounty to man, and such a proof as arises from it of man's obligation to God, should be thus abused. From the highest heavens, it is certain, God beholds all the children of men; to them he has given the earth; but to the children of God heaven is given. 2. The dead are not capable of praising him (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">v. 17</reference>), nor <hi type="italic">any that go into silence.</hi> The soul indeed lives in a state of separation from the body and is capable of praising God; and <hi type="italic">the souls of the faithful, after they are delivered from the burdens of the flesh,</hi> do praise God, are still praising him; for they go up to the land of perfect light and constant business. But the dead body cannot praise God; death puts an end to our glorifying God in this world of trial and conflict, to all our services in the field; the grave is a land of darkness and silence, where there is no work or device. This they plead with God for deliverance out of the hand of their enemies, "Lord, if they prevail to cut us off, the idols will carry the day, and there will be none to praise thee, to bear thy name, and to bear a testimony against the worshippers of idols." <hi type="italic">The dead praise not the Lord,</hi> so as we do in the business and for the comforts of this life. See <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Ps. xxx. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.10">lxxxviii. 10</reference>. 3. Therefore it concerns us to praise him (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But we,</hi> we that are alive, <hi type="italic">will bless the Lord;</hi> we and those that shall come after us, will do it, <hi type="italic">from this time forth and for evermore,</hi> to the end of time; we and those we shall remove to, <hi type="italic">from this time forth</hi> and to eternity. <hi type="italic">The dead praise not the Lord,</hi> therefore we will do it the more diligently." (1.) Others are dead, and an end is thereby put to their service, and therefore we will lay out ourselves to do so much the more for God, that we may fill up the gap. <hi type="italic">Moses my servant is dead, now therefore, Joshua, arise.</hi> (2.) We ourselves must shortly go to the land of silence; <hi type="italic">but, while we do live, we will bless the Lord,</hi> will improve our time and work that work of him that sent us into the world to praise him before the night comes, and because <hi type="italic">the night comes, wherein no man can work. The Lord will bless us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.12">v. 12</reference>); he will do well for us, and therefore <hi type="italic">we will bless</hi> him, we will speak well of him. Poor returns for such receivings! Nay, we will not only do it ourselves, but will engage others to do it. <hi type="italic">Praise the Lord;</hi> praise him with us; praise him in your places, as we in ours; praise him when we are gone, that he may be praised <hi type="italic">for evermore. Hallelujah.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.115"/> <div eID="gen12580" type="x-p"/>

entries.8618f9724cf99d1d0c7895db48448d189b6e3c1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6834"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 115</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.115.1-Ps.115.18">Psa 115:1-18</reference>. The Psalmist prays that God would vindicate His glory, which is contrasted with the vanity of idols, while the folly of their worshippers is contrasted with the trust of God's people, who are encouraged to its exercise and to unite in the praise which it occasions.</title> <div sID="gen10494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6834"/>1-3. The vindication of God's mercy and faithfulness (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.10">Psa 25:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">36:6</reference>) is the "glory" of His "name," which is desired to be illustrated in the deliverance of His people, as the implied mode of its manifestation. In view of the taunts of the heathen, faith in His dominion as enthroned in the heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.4">11:4</reference>) is avowed. <div eID="gen10494" type="x-p"/>
entries.266ab1b7ec75d179c444f0e857193cdb3001b90a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6836"/><div sID="gen10496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6836"/>4-7. (Compare Is 40:18-20; 44:9-20). <div eID="gen10496" type="x-p"/>
entries.63e882e3ba4ec2860d19d9e40176ac0e64b5a2ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6838"/><div sID="gen10498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6838"/><hi type="bold">8. every one that trusteth--</hi>they who trust, whether makers or not. <div eID="gen10498" type="x-p"/>
entries.2975bdeae05c5aa2ae92384d70a432146c3d277c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6839"/><div sID="gen10499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6839"/>9-13. The repetitions imply earnestness. <div eID="gen10499" type="x-p"/>
entries.892b89cb5740aeca8f7ce08fe66e90bfc60badce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6840"/><div sID="gen10500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6840"/>14. Opposed to the decrease pending and during the captivity. <div eID="gen10500" type="x-p"/>
entries.05be59734f89818f079548423bcda40f2d043884: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6841"/><div sID="gen10501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6841"/>15-17. They were not only God's peculiar people, but as living inhabitants of earth, assigned the work of His praise as monuments of divine power, wisdom, and goodness. <div eID="gen10501" type="x-p"/>
entries.64afc1991c67aaa45096b561c256094fcf27d917: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6842"/><div sID="gen10502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6842"/>18. Hence let us fulfil the purpose of our creation, and evermore show forth His praise. <chapter eID="Ps.115"/>

entries.0d0e18733d9db5d59e9d686b413b9ff25cadb8d6: <div eID="gen22563" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22564" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22565" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22565" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22564" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22566" type="x-p"/> God alone is to be glorified, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.1-Psa.115.3">Psa 115:1-3</reference>. The vanity of idols, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.4-Psa.115.8">Psa 115:4-8</reference>. Israel, the house of Aaron, and all that fear God, are exhorted to trust it the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.9-Psa.115.11">Psa 115:9-11</reference>. The Lord's goodness to his people, and his gracious promises, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.12-Psa.115.16">Psa 115:12-16</reference>. As the dead cannot praise him, the living should, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.17">Psa 115:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.115.18">Psa 115:18</reference>. <div eID="gen22566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22567" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is written as a part of the preceding by eighteen of Kennicott's and fifty-three of De Rossi's MSS.; by some ancient editions the Septuagint, the Syriac, the Vulgate, the Ethiopic, the Arabic, and the Anglo-Saxon. The old Anglo-Scottish Psalter reads it consecutively with the foregoing. Who the author of both was, we know not, nor on what occasion it was written. It seems to be an epinikion or triumphal song, in which the victory gained is entirely ascribed to Jehovah. <div eID="gen22567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22568" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22569" type="x-p"/> Not unto us, O Lord - We take no merit to ourselves; as thine is the kingdom, and the power in that kingdom, so is thy glory. <div eID="gen22569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22570" type="x-p"/> For thy mercy, and for thy truth's sake - Thy mercy gave thy promise, thy truth fulfilled it.
entries.31f7958795d3d026d8e73762656a78dafac6b8cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22571" type="x-p"/> Wherefore should the heathen say - This appears to refer to a time in which the Israelites had suffered some sad reverses, so as to be brought very low, and to be marked by the heathen.
entries.9d2fd22fc040511f2b3c1291021fc4d7108aa397: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22572" type="x-p"/> He hath done whatsover he hath pleased - There was too much cause for his abandoning us to our enemies; yet he still lives and rules in heaven and in earth.
entries.7b8dd079b087ed120eca30699a52565a323d8e5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22573" type="x-p"/> Their idols are silver, etc. - They are metal, stone, and wood. They are generally made in the form of man, but can neither see, hear, smell, feel, walk, nor speak. How brutish to trust in such! And next to these, in stupidity and inanity, must they be who form them, with the expectation of deriving any good from them. So obviously vain was the whole system of idolatry, that the more serious heathens ridiculed it, and it was a butt for the jests of their freethinkers and buffoons. How keen are those words of Juvenal! - - Audis Jupiter, haec? nec labra moves, cum mittere vocem. <div eID="gen22573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22574" type="x-p"/> Debueras, vel marmoreus vel aheneus? aut cur <div eID="gen22574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22575" type="x-p"/> In carbone tuo charta pia thura soluta <div eID="gen22575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22576" type="x-p"/> Ponimus, et sectum vituli jecur, albaque porci <div eID="gen22576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22577" type="x-p"/> Omenta? ut video, nullum discrimen habendum est. <div eID="gen22577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22578" type="x-p"/> Effigies inter vestras, statuamque Bathylli. <div eID="gen22578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22579" type="x-p"/> Sat. xiii., ver. 113. <div eID="gen22579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22580" type="x-p"/> Dost thou hear, O Jupiter, these things? nor move thy lips when thou oughtest to speak out, whether thou art of marble or of bronze? Or, why do we put the sacred incense on thy altar from the opened paper, and the extracted liver of a calf, and the white caul of a hog? As far as I can discern there is no difference between thy statue and that of Bathyllus." <div eID="gen22580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22581" type="x-p"/> This irony will appear the keener, when it is known that Bathyllus was a fiddler and player, whose image by the order of Polycrates, was erected in the temple of Juno at Samos. See <reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Isa 41:1</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.7">Isa 46:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.4">Jer 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">Jer 10:5</reference>, etc.; and <reference osisRef="Psa.135.15">Psa 135:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.135.16">Psa 135:16</reference>.
entries.92b9a2c32bffae7bad441b5d4bf58670436c470f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22582" type="x-p"/> O Israel - The body of the Jewish people.
entries.861692a40d393207d1f4a54f153aaffa9d8416ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22583" type="x-p"/> O house of Aaron - All the different classes of the priesthood.
entries.8cb4489aa9bf24875c8c4f709af8e27bee30c2df: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22584" type="x-p"/> Ye that fear the Lord - All real penitents, and sincere believers, trust to the Lord, in the almighty, omniscient, and infinitely good Jehovah. <div eID="gen22584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22585" type="x-p"/> He is their help and shield - He is the succor, support, guardian, and defense of all who put their confidence in him.
entries.5fa9c39d3a582a97610d2d68e92c81029bf2b5cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22586" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath been mindful - He has never yet wholly abandoned us to our enemies. <div eID="gen22586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22587" type="x-p"/> He will bless the house of Israel - He will bless the people as a nation; he will bless the priesthood and Levites; he will bless all of them who fear him, great and small, in whatsoever station or circumstances found. There is a great deal of emphasis in this verse: several words are redoubled to make the subject the more affecting. I give a literal translation: - <reference osisRef="Psa.115.12">Psa 115:12</reference> "The Lord has been mindful of us he will bless the house of Israel; she will bless the house of Aaron. <reference osisRef="Psa.115.13">Psa 115:13</reference> He will bless them that fear Jehovah, the small with the great. <reference osisRef="Psa.115.14">Psa 115:14</reference> Jehovah will add upon you, upon you and upon all your children. <reference osisRef="Psa.115.15">Psa 115:15</reference> Blessed are ye of the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth. <reference osisRef="Psa.115.16">Psa 115:16</reference> The heavens of heavens are the Lord's: but the earth he hath given to the sons of Adam." <div eID="gen22587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22588" type="x-p"/> Jehovah is absolute Master of the universe. He has made the heavens of heavens, and also the earth; and this he gives to the children of Adam. When he exiled him from paradise, he turned him out into the earth, and gave it to him and his sons for ever, that they might dress, till, and eat of its produce all their days.
entries.9ae89062d21414e10219949b5c8daeb09f2d2cfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22589" type="x-p"/> The dead praise not the Lord - המתים hammethim, those dead men who worshipped as gods dumb idols, dying in their sins, worship not Jehovah; nor can any of those who go down into silence praise thee: earth is the place in which to praise the Lord for his mercies, and get a preparation for his glory.
entries.fcf2a0d717b076188c21d43e6a11d90ea461da76: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen22589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22590" type="x-p"/> But we will bless the Lord - Our fathers, who received so much from thy bounty, are dead, their tongues are silent in the grave; we are in their place, and wish to magnify thy name, for thou hast dealt bountifully with us. But grant us those farther blessings before we die which we so much need; and we will praise thee as living monuments of thy mercy, and the praise we begin now shall continue for ever and ever. <div eID="gen22590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22591" type="x-p"/> The Targum, for "neither any that go down into silence," has "nor any that descend into the house of earthly sepulture," that is, the tomb. The Anglo-Saxon: neither all they that go down into hell. Nogh the dede sal loue the Lorde, ne al that lyghtes in hell. Old Psalter. The word hell among our ancestors meant originally the covered, or hidden obscure place, from helan, to cover or conceal: it now expresses only the place of endless torment.  <chapter eID="Ps.115"/> <div eID="gen22591" type="x-p"/>

entries.1646d8557b8cbae0c5e878ae779bd055cfd1145e: <div eID="gen10094" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Call to the God of Israel, the Living God, to Rescue the Honour of His Name</title> <div sID="gen10095" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, which has scarcely anything in common with the preceding Psalm except that the expression “house of Jacob,” <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1">Psa 114:1</reference>, is here broken up into its several members in Psa 115:12., is found joined with it, making one Psalm, in the lxx, Syriac, Arabic and Aethiopic versions, just as on the other hand Ps 116 is split up into two. This arbitrary arrangement condemns itself. Nevertheless Kimchi favours it, and it has found admission into not a few Hebrew manuscripts. <div eID="gen10095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10096" type="x-p"/> It is a prayer of Israel for God’s aid, probably in the presence of an expedition against heathen enemies. The two middle strophes of the four are of the same compass. Ewald’s conjecture, that whilst the Psalm was being sung the sacrifice was proceeded with, and that in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.12">Psa 115:12</reference> the voice of a priest proclaims the gracious acceptance of the sacrifice, is pleasing. But the change of voices begins even with <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9">Psa 115:9</reference>, as Olshausen also supposes.
entries.e60d3cfdaae3b45deece1fac3116e4772d9f1fff: <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1-Ps.115.2">Psa 115:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10097" type="x-p"/> It has to do not so much with the honour of Israel, which is not worthy of the honour (Eze 36:22.) and has to recognise in its reproach a well-merited chastisement, as with the honour of Him who cannot suffer the reproaching of His holy name to continue long. He willeth that His name should be sanctified. In the consciousness of his oneness with this will, the poet bases his petition, in so far as it is at the same time a petition on behalf of Israel, upon God’s cha'ris and alee'theia as upon two columns. The second על, according to an express note of the Masora, has no <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> before it, although the lxx and Targum insert one. The thought in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Psa 115:2</reference> is moulded after <reference osisRef="Ps.79.10">Psa 79:10</reference>, or after <reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>; Mic 7:10. איּה־נא is the same style as נגדּה־נּא in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.18">Psa 116:18</reference>, cf. in the older language אל־נא, אם־נא, and the like.
entries.a1b72dfb4378145aa4fc7effd30fbff2f7d195aa: <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3-Ps.115.8">Psa 115:3-8</reference> <div eID="gen10097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10098" type="x-p"/> The poet, with “And our God,” in the name of Israel opposes the scornful question of the heathen by the believingly joyous confession of the exaltation of Jahve above the false gods. Israel’s God is in the heavens, and is therefore supramundane in nature and life, and the absolutely unlimited One, who is able to do all things with a freedom that is conditioned only by Himself: <hi type="italic">quod vult, valet</hi> (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference></hi> = <reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">Psa 135:6</reference>, Wisd. 12:18, and frequently). The carved gods (עצב, from עצב, cogn. חצב, קצב) of the heathen, on the contrary, are dead images, which are devoid of all life, even of the sensuous life the outward organs of which are imagined upon them. It cannot be proved with <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Ecc 5:16</reference> that ידיהם and רגליחם are equivalent to ידים להם, רגלים. They are either subjects which the <hi type="italic">Waw apodosis</hi> cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.22.24">Gen 22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.24">Pro 23:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Hab 2:5</reference>) renders prominent, or <hi type="italic">casus absoluti</hi> (Ges. §145, 2), since both verbs have the idols themselves as their subjects less on account of their gender (יד and רגל are feminine, but the Hebrew usage of genders is very free and not carried out uniformly) as in respect of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference></hi>: with reference to their hands, etc. ימישׁוּן is the energetic future form, which goes over from משׁשׁ into מוּשׁ, for ימשּׁוּ. It is said once again in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.115.7">Psa 115:7</reference></hi> that speech is wanting to them; for the other negations only deny life to them, this at the same time denies all personality. The author might know from his own experience how little was the distinction made by the heathen worship between the symbol and the thing symbolized. Accordingly the worship of idols seems to him, as to the later prophets, to be the extreme of self-stupefaction and of the destruction of human consciousness; and the final destiny of the worshippers of false gods, as he says in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">Psa 115:8</reference>, is, that they become like to their idols, that is to say, being deprived of their consciousness, life, and existence, they come to nothing, like those their nothingnesses (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference>). This whole section of the Psalm is repeated in Ps 135 (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.6">Psa 115:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.15">Psa 115:15</reference>).
entries.7ca4496967f8980ce04c05596a677f7882f90fb8: <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9-Ps.115.14">Psa 115:9-14</reference> <div eID="gen10098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10099" type="x-p"/> After this confession of Israel there now arises a voice that addresses itself to Israel. The threefold division into Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear Jahve is the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.2">Psa 118:2</reference>-4. In Ps 135 the “house of Levi” is further added to the house of Aaron. Those who fear Jahve, who also stand in the last passage, are probably the proselytes (in the Acts of the Apostles σεβόμενοι τὸν Θεόν, or merely σεβόμενοι)<note placement="foot">The appellation φοβούμενοι does not however occur, if we do not bring <reference osisRef="Acts.10.2">Act 10:2</reference> in here; but in Latin inscriptions in Orelli-Hentzen No. 2523, and in Auer in the <hi type="italic">Zeitschrift für katholische Theologie</hi> 1852, S. 80, the proselyte <hi type="italic">(religionis Judaicae</hi>) is called <hi type="italic">metuens</hi>.)</note> at any rate these are included even if Israel in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.9">Psa 115:9</reference> is meant to signify the laity, for the notion of “those who fear Jahve” extends beyond Israel. The fact that the threefold refrain of the summons does not run, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">Psa 33:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">our help and shield is He</hi>, is to be explained from its being an antiphonal song. In so far, however, as the Psalm supplicates God’s protection and help in a campaign the declaration of confident hope, <hi type="italic">their help and shield is He</hi>, may, with Hitzig, be referred to the army that is gone or is going forth. It is the same voice which bids Israel to be of good courage and announces to the people the well-pleased acceptance of the sacrifice with the words “Jahve hath been mindful of us” (זכרנוּ ה, cf. עתּה ידעתּי, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>), perhaps simultaneously with the presentation of the memorial portion (אזכרה) of the meat-offering (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">Psa 38:1</reference>). The יברך placed at the head is particularized threefold, corresponding to the threefold summons. The special promise of blessing which is added in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.14">Psa 115:14</reference> is an echo of <reference osisRef="Deut.1.11">Deu 1:11</reference>, as in 2Sa 24:3. The contracted future יסף we take in a consolatory sense; for as an optative it would be too isolated here. In spite of all oppression on the part of the heathen, God will make His people ever more numerous, more capable of offering resistance, and more awe-inspiring.
entries.4248a5d32f17f4b2487404ba10f6b7f40dbbef82: <reference osisRef="Ps.115.15-Ps.115.18">Psa 115:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen10099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10100" type="x-p"/> The voice of consolation is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.15">Psa 115:15</reference>, but it becomes the voice of hope by being blended with the newly strengthened believing tone of the congregation. Jahve is here called the Creator of heaven and earth because the worth and magnitude of His blessing are measured thereby. He has reserved the heavens to Himself, but given the earth to men. This separation of heaven and earth is a fundamental characteristic of the post-diluvian history. The throne of God is in the heavens, and the promise, which is given to the patriarchs on behalf of all mankind, does not refer to heaven, but to the possession of the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.22">Psa 37:22</reference>). The promise is as yet limited to this present world, whereas in the New Testament this limitation is removed and the κληρονομία embraces heaven and earth. This Old Testament limitedness finds further expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">Psa 115:17</reference>, where דּוּמה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.17">Psa 94:17</reference>, signifies the silent land of Hades. The Old Testament knows nothing of a heavenly <hi type="italic">ecclesia</hi> that praises God without intermission, consisting not merely of angels, but also of the spirits of all men who die in the faith. Nevertheless there are not wanting hints that point upwards which were even better understood by the post-exilic than by the pre-exilic church. The New Testament morn began to dawn even upon the post-exilic church. We must not therefore be astonished to find the tone of <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11-Ps.88.13">Psa 88:11-13</reference>, struck up here, although the echo of those earlier Psalms here is only the dark foil of the confession which the church makes in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.18">Psa 115:18</reference> concerning its immortality. The church of Jahve as such does not die. That it also does not remain among the dead, in whatever degree it may die off in its existing members, the psalmist might know from <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>; Isa 25:8. But the close of the Psalm shows that such predictions which light up the life beyond only gradually became elements of the church’s consciousness, and, so to speak, dogmas.  <chapter eID="Ps.115"/> <div eID="gen10100" type="x-p"/>

entries.d6097b5a5c9a90a5616d54f82771c6b7ea6d778b:
PSALM 115
It is obvious that this psalm was penned when the Church was deeply afflicted. Unworthy as they are to be heard by God, the faithful, nevertheless, offer up supplications to him for deliverance, lest his holy name might be exposed to scorn and reproach among the heathen. Then, mustering courage, they mock at the madness of all who are addicted to the worship of idols; and, with holy boasting, they magnify their own happiness, in that they have been adopted by God; and from this also they take occasion to stimulate one another to acknowledge the kindness which they have received from him.
Psalm 115:1-3
1. Not unto us, O Jehovah! not unto us, but unto thy name give the glory, on account of thy mercy, on account of thy truth. 2. Why should the heathen say, Where is now their God? 3. Surely our God is in heaven: he hath done whatsoever pleased him.
 
1 Not unto us, O Jehovah! It is not certain by whom, or at what time, this psalm was composed.
“As the former psalm ended abruptly, and this is connected with it by the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Æthiopic, with nineteen MSS.; and as the following ejaculations so naturally arise from the consideration of the wonderful works of Jehovah just before recited, Lorinus’s opinion, that it is only a continuation of the former, is not improbable. Patrick refers it to 2 Chronicles 20:2. Some suppose it to be written by Moses at the Red Sea. Others, by David in the beginning of his reign. Others, by Mordecai and Esther. Others, by the three children in the fiery furnace. Perhaps by Hezekiah, or some one in the Babylonish captivity. — See Psalm 114:1.” — Dimoch. “There is nothing certain,” observes Walford, “to be concluded respecting the author of this psalm, or the occasion on which it was written. It is conjectured, however, to belong to the time of Hezekiah, and to have been composed in celebration of the very extraordinary deliverance which was afforded to that pious prince, and to his people, from the blasphemies and arrogance of Sennacherib, the king of Assyria, 2 Chronicles 32; Isaiah 37:37. Whether this conjecture be agreeable to the truth, we are unable to say, though a considerable probability that it is so, arises from the language of the psalm itself.”
We learn from the first part of it, that the faithful betake themselves to God, in circumstances of extreme distress. They do not make known their desires in plain words, but indirectly hint at the nature of their request. They openly disclaim all merit, and all hope of obtaining deliverance otherwise than God’s doing it from a sole regard to his own glory, for these things are inseparably connected. Deserving, therefore, to meet with a repulse, they yet beseech God not to expose his name to the derision of the heathen. In their distress they desire to obtain consolation and support; but, finding nothing in themselves meritorious of God’s favor, they call upon him to grant their requests, that his glory may be maintained. This is a point to which we ought carefully to attend, that, altogether unworthy as we are of God’s regard, we may cherish the hope of being saved by him, from the respect that he has for the glory of his name, and from his having adopted us on condition of never forsaking us. It must, also be noticed, that their humility and modesty prevent them from openly complaining of their distresses, and that they do not begin with a request for their own deliverance, but for the glory of God. Suffused with shame by reason of their calamity, which, in itself, amounts to a kind of rejection, they durst not openly crave, at God’s hand, what they wished, but made their appeal indirectly, that, from a regard to his own glory, he would prove a father to sinners, who had no claim upon him whatever. And, as this formulary of prayer has once been delivered to the Church, let us also, in all our approaches unto God, remember to lay aside all self-righteousness, and to place our hopes entirely on his free favor. Moreover, when we pray for help, we ought to have the glory of God in view, in the deliverance which we obtain. And it is most likely they adopted this form of prayer, being led to do so by the promise. For, during the captivity, God had said, “Not for your sake, but for mine own sake will I do this,” Isaiah 48:11. When all other hopes fail, they acknowledge this to be their only refuge. The repetition of it is an evidence how conscious they were of their own demerit, so that, if their prayers should happen to be rejected a hundred times, they could not, in their own name, prefer any charge against him.

entries.41eee1aadf7c38605519c98c3070f294c6aeac42:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="115" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The occasion of this Psalm was to manifest some eminent dan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger or distress of the people of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> from some Idolatrous Nations. But whether it was that mentioned 2 <ns0:hi>Chron</ns0:hi> 20. or what other, is but matter of conjecture, and not worth our inqui<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>y.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 NOt unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy Name give glory <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">As we intreat thy favour and aid, and that thou wouldst work gloriously on our behalf to bring us out of our present straits and extremities, so we do not desire this out of a vain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />glorious humor, as usually men do in such cases, that we may get renown by the conquest of our proud and mighty ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies, but that thy honour may be vindicated from all their contempts and blasphemies; and if thou wilt deliver us, we will not arrogate the praise and glory of it to our own worth or valour, but onely to thy <ns0:hi>mercy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>truth,</ns0:hi> as it follows.</ns0:note>, for thy mercy, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> for thy truths sake.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Wherefore should the heathen say <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Why dost thou suffer them, or give them any colour or occasion to say or think so, by conniving at their wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and by giving thy people into their hands?</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 423. 10, & 79. 10. Joel 2. 17.</ns0:note> Where is now <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He is no where, he is lost or at a loss either unable or unwilling or not at leisure to save them.</ns0:note> their God <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Who hath undertaken to be their God and Saviour, and whom they onely worship, and of whom they use to boast and insult over us and over our Gods.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 135. 6.</ns0:note> But our God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Whom, notwithstanding your reproaches, we are not ashamed to owne for our God.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the heavens <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Although he have no vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sible shape nor bodily presence with us here upon earth, as your Idols have, which is a certain proof of their baseness and weakness, yet he hath a certain and a glorious place where he resideth, even the highest heavens, where he is cloathed with infinite Power and Majesty, and from whence he beholdeth and governeth this lower world, and all that is in it.</ns0:note>, he hath done whatsoever he pleased <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>he doth,</ns0:hi> &c. By his onely will and pleasure all things were at first made, and are still disposed, and without this nothing cometh to pass. And therefore all your insolencies and injuries and successes against us do not come from an invincible power in you or in your Idols, nor from any defect of strength or goodness in our God, but onely from hence, that it pleased him for many wise and holy rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons to afflict us, and to give you prosperity for a time.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 4. 28. Psal. 135. 15. Jer. 10. 3, &c.</ns0:note> Their idols <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> silver and gold <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Thus glorious and powerful is our God, O ye heathens, of whom you so boldly ask, who and where he is: but as for your Gods or Idols, they have no power nor worth in them, but what is taken from their materials.</ns0:note>, the work of mens hands <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As their matter is wholly from the earth, so their form or figure they have from the art of man; and therefore they should rather, if it were possible, worship man, as their Creator and Lord than be worshipped by him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 They have mouths, but they speak not <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">For although the blind Heathen are by their Idolatrous Priests made to believe otherwise concerning their Idols, in regard of the Spirits which they pretend to dwell in them, yet this is the truth of the matter, and confirmed by long and constant experience, that they are but vain and senceless things, they can neither <ns0:hi>speak</ns0:hi> in answer to your prayers or inquiries, nor <ns0:hi>see</ns0:hi> what you do or what you want; nor <ns0:hi>hear</ns0:hi> your petitions; nor <ns0:hi>smell</ns0:hi> your incenses and sacrifices; nor <ns0:hi>handle</ns0:hi> or use their hands either to take any thing from you, or to give any thing to you; nor so much as <ns0:hi>mutte<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> or give the least signification of their apprehension of your condi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion and concerns.</ns0:note>, eyes have they, but they see not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:502" />6 They have ears, but they hear not; noses have they, but they smell not.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 They have hands, but they handle not; feet have they, but they walk not; neither speak <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>mutter,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>make a noise,</ns0:hi> as this word signifies <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 13. 14. They are so far from speaking with their throat and other instruments of speech, as men do, that they cannot make such an inarticulate and senceless sound with them, as the beasts do.</ns0:note> they through their throat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 They that make them <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>they that observe</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>worship them.</ns0:hi> For the Psalmists quarrel was not so much with those few Artists who formed the Images, as with all the adorers of them. And the word here rendred <ns0:hi>make</ns0:hi> doth sometimes signifie to <ns0:hi>worship,</ns0:hi> as some understand it, not without probability, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 32. 35. <ns0:hi>because they made (i. e.</ns0:hi> worshipped) <ns0:hi>the calf which Aaron made,</ns0:hi> and as in other Languages words answering to this do signifie, as hath been oft observed by learned men; and it oft signifies to <ns0:hi>observe;</ns0:hi> as when men are said <ns0:hi>to make</ns0:hi> (as it is in the Hebrew) <ns0:hi>the Sabbath, Deut.</ns0:hi> 5. 15. and <ns0:hi>the release,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the Passover,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the feast of weeks,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 15. 1. & 16. 1. 10.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>let them be like unto them.</ns0:hi> So Gr.</ns0:note> are like unto them <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This is a sharp reflection, either 1. upon the Idols, whose highest preferment it is to be made like unto man, a mortal, weak and miserable creature, infinitely in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feriour to the true God. Or, 2. to the makers or wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shippers of them, who by this absurd and foolish action, shew that they are as ignorant and stupid and void of all sence and reason as their Images.</ns0:note>; <ns0:hi>so is</ns0:hi> every one that trusteth in them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 O Israel <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Do not thou follow the example of these brutish Idola<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters, but serve the Lord onely.</ns0:note>, trust thou in the LORD: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> their help <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Who trust in God, as he now required. Or, <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>your</ns0:hi> by a change of per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons, which is most frequent in Scripture, and especially in these Books.</ns0:note> and their shield.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 O house of Aaron <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">You Priests and Levites proceeding from <ns0:hi>Aaron,</ns0:hi> or re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lated to him, who have special reason and many obligations to do it, who have a more distinct knowledge of God, which is the foundation of trust, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 9. 10. and who are to be both instructers of and examples to the people in this as well as in other duties.</ns0:note>, trust in the LORD: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> their help and their shield.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Ye that fear the LORD <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">All and every one of you who worship the true God, not onely Aaronites and Israelites, but even Gentile-prose<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lytes, who are said to <ns0:hi>come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel, Ruth</ns0:hi> 2. 12. And such there were many at this time in the Church of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> whom therefore he fitly invites to trust God, because he is no less their, than the Israelites, help and shield, as it follows.</ns0:note>, trust in the LORD: he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> their help and their shield.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 The LORD hath been mindful of us <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">In our former straits and calamities, and therefore we trust he <ns0:hi>will</ns0:hi> still <ns0:hi>bless us,</ns0:hi> &c. as it follows. Or, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>will be mindful of us.</ns0:hi> Though he hath chastened us sore, yet he hath not yet cast us out of the care of his providence.</ns0:note>, he will bless <ns0:hi>us,</ns0:hi> he will bless the house of Israel, he will bless the house of Aaron.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 He will bless them that fear the LORD, <ns0:hi>both</ns0:hi> small <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> with.</ns0:note> and great <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either in age or condition, of whatsoever quality, high and low, rich and poor; for he is no respecter of persons.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 The LORD shall increase you <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In number, notwithstanding all the attempts of your enemies to diminish and destroy you. Or, <ns0:hi>shall add to you,</ns0:hi> to wit, further and greater blessings.</ns0:note> more and more, you and your children.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> blessed of the LORD, which made heaven and earth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Who therefore can bless you indeed in spight of all your enemies curses and oppositions; and not of an impotent Idol that can do you neither good nor hurt.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 The heaven, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> the heavens <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the LORD's <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To wit, in a peculiar manner, where he dwelleth in that light and glory to which no man can approach, and whence he beholdeth and disposeth all persons and things upon earth.</ns0:note>: but the earth hath he given to the children of men <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">For their habitation, possession and use. But these words may be and are thus rendred by others, <ns0:hi>and the earth</ns0:hi> which (which particle is very oft understood) <ns0:hi>he hath given,</ns0:hi> &c. And then as the foregoing verse declared that God was the Creator of Heaven and Earth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 15. so this asserts that he is also their Lord and Governor to dispose of all men and things as he pleaseth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 88. 10, 11, 12. Isa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 38. 18.</ns0:note> The dead <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Such as we shall suddenly be, if thou dost not succour us.</ns0:note> praise not the LORD, nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther any that go down into <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Psal. 94. 17.</ns0:note> silence <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Into the place of silence, the grave.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 2. 20.</ns0:note> But we will bless the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">But we hope for better things, that notwithstanding our present and urgent danger, yet thou wilt deliver us, and so give us occasion to bless thy Name; whereby thou wilt have the praise and glory of our deliverance.</ns0:note>; from this time forth and for evermore. Praise the LORD.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
